_rules: Every pipeline follows the run protocol (core/run.mjs): start, pull, compute, apply, end; each move prints the exact calls.

A step is code (core/steps.mjs CODE_STEPS), or agent: a named judgment, the material it is shown, the shape of its answer and the fold that turns the answer into writes. Code does every step with one right answer.
reads is the pull: the collections a run reads, with windowDays where only recent documents matter. The journal is in no read set (D-059).
steps null means the pipeline's steps arrive with the backlog task in pendingIn; its task is not created before then.

steps.does: plans the day, picks the weak spots due for review, the new checks and the drills the plan calls for, and finds the passages in his materials each one rests on

steps.judgment: Write today's review and drill questions from the brief: one review item per target weak spot (from a new angle if it has history), one check per objective listed, and each drill's count of items on its chapters and objectives. Ground every item in the passages given; match their terms and values. Each item: type single|sata|matrix (numeric only in a numeric drill), stem (10+ characters), options (2 to 6) and correct (indexes) or a matrix, rationales, objective, topic, cjStep (one of the six clinical-judgment steps), sourceRef (materials/<id> it rests on) or verify: true when the point is not in his materials; a review item names its weakspotId target; never select-N; only exam content. A drill marked numeric is a dosage drill (D-100): only type numeric items, each with stem (the order, what is on hand, and the rounding asked for), answer (a number), unit (one of spec.items.units), tolerance (half the rounding step: 0.05 for tenths, 0.5 for whole drops; 0 when exact), steps (the worked solution, one line each), objective, topic, cjStep and sourceRef (one of that drill's passages); work the numbers from the passages' methods; never from his medication table or drug cards. A calculation question (a dose, mL per dose, tablets, a rate in mL/hr, drops per minute, a unit conversion) also carries calc, the numbers from its stem that its answer is worked from: weightKg or weightLb; dosePerKg with per "day" or "dose" and, for per day, dosesPerDay or everyHours; or dose (the ordered amount); doseUnit (mg, mcg, g or units); stockAmount, stockUnit and stockMl for what is on hand (100 mg per 5 mL is stockAmount 100, stockUnit mg, stockMl 5; a tablet is stockForm "tablet" with no stockMl); volumeMl with hours or minutes, and dropFactor (gtt/mL) for drops per minute; or value, from and to for a conversion. E.V. works the answer from calc and drops a question whose key is not that answer, or whose options do not hold it: work the numbers first, then write the options with the answer among them, and never let a rationale disagree with the key. The stem only asks the question: it never holds the answer, the working or "Answer:"; the working goes only in calc and the rationale.

steps.judgment: Check, read-only, that this record runs the build it should: make each listed read exactly as listed, in order, and save each result as its note says, with the printed tool-result command, never retyped. When list_triggers returns a next_cursor, call it again with the same arguments plus that cursor and save the next page the same way, until there is none. Change nothing. Answer saved: true when every read was made and saved; if a read is refused, stop there and answer saved: false with the refusal quoted.

Write the week's review for Matt from the brief: what moved, what is still weak (nearest exam first), the coming week's dates, any failed runs, one suggestion for next week; then one reflection question for him to write about, and a one-line push. The brief's insights are the week's numbers, computed by code (B-72): say in a sentence or two what they mean for next week (the weakest objective, an item missed every time, what keeps coming back, how study minutes sat against the next day's accuracy); quote them, never recompute or round them differently. Plain, warm, under 3000 characters.

steps.judgment: Bring Canvas in, read-only, as the material says: find the Canvas tab in the built-in browser (open one if there is none); if it shows a sign-in page, stop and answer signed-out (never sign in). Then for each part in order (dates, files, then each texts batch): print its script with the command given, run the printed script with javascript_tool in the Canvas tab (it returns at once with 'started <part>'), then print and run the part's poll script every 15 seconds or so until it stops saying 'still running'. The poll result is long on purpose, so the tool saves it to a file and names it; run the unwrap command on that file. Never retype a result. Answer ok when dates and files were collected (and every texts batch, if any), otherwise the status that fits, with the problem in one line.

Write the one short note Matt sees about tonight's Canvas sync, plain and warm, at most two sentences. For each possible conflict, say only that two entries disagree and that he should check with his instructor; never pick a side, and leave out anything that is not a real conflict. On Saturdays, read his Quizlet home page as the material says and name the one deck most worth refreshing for the coming week's exams and open weak spots.

diagnostic.purpose: runs the one probe named in the firing text and records what it found, so a capability is proven before anything is built on it

input.probe: the probe, from the message that started this run ('Probe: <what to find out>')

_rules: A named probe ('Probe: <name>') is a measurement: compute writes its probe documents to files and prints the exact calls, which are the only record writes a diagnostic makes, all into debug/<run id>-<label>. Any other probe is answered with read-only commands.
Groups run in order; within a group the calls go from smallest to largest and stop at the first refusal, so nothing beyond the ceiling is attempted twice.

ceilings.measures: the largest document one ArtifactData set accepts and the batch ceilings (writes per batch, bytes per batch)

groups.name: document
groups.rule: one set per call, ascending; stop at the first refusal

groups.name: batch-writes
groups.rule: one batch of many small writes

groups.name: batch-bytes
groups.rule: batches of documents just under the document limit, ascending total; stop at the first refusal

cloud-reads.measures: whether a cloud run can read its record's page with the Artifact tool (the stored declaration and the published files) and list this account's scheduled tasks with list_triggers: the two reads the weekly's verify step needs (B-29)

groups.name: artifact-read
groups.rule: one read of this record's page; note whether it answered and whether the result held the <artifact-stored-declaration> block

groups.name: list-triggers
groups.rule: one read of the enabled tasks; note whether it answered and how many it listed

page-publish.measures: whether a cloud run can publish a new private Artifact page and get its link back: the call a share-set job needs (B-54, D-110). The page is made up and holds no study data

groups.name: publish
groups.rule: one publish of the made-up page the run wrote; note whether it was accepted, the link it returned, or the refusal in its words

steps.judgment: Find out exactly what the probe asks. When the material lists calls, make them exactly as listed, group by group in order, stopping a group at its first refused call, and note for each call whether it was accepted or refused and the refusal's words; make no other record call. Otherwise use read-only commands in this session (no record writes, no network beyond what the probe names, nothing deleted). Report what you observed, not what you expect: findings in at most 480 characters, each capability you saw work (proven), each limit you hit (limits), and any measured number (numbers, e.g. documentKiBAccepted).

to is a collection, a spec map (spec.courses), named (the value is <collection>/<id>, the ideas link shape and a passage's sourceRef; a prefix that is no collection, as note/ for his note's line, points outside the record and is not checked) or plans.tasks (a task id inside any plan). link is required, optional or external: lint (core/lint.mjs through core/links.mjs) reports a dangling required link as an error and a dangling optional one as a note; an external link points outside the record and is not checked.

tools/build.mjs refuses a row naming a collection or field the schemas lack, or a target that is no collection and no spec map. linked(db, doc, field) in core/links.mjs resolves one document's link. weakspots.origin.item is left out: an item lives inside its set. weakspots.links[].to is named, like the ideas link (B-232); lint also fails a duplicate-of that names no weak spot, itself or another duplicate (D-240).

exam-plan.instructions:
# Study Plan Maker: best-practices brief

You are building an agent that makes study plans for one student and one course. This brief is what it should know: how a plan is organized, the approach that works, the rubric it checks itself against, and the rules it never breaks. The core works for any course. Course profiles at the end add what a nursing course or a biology course needs on top.

The approach and rubric were tested: three versions of the same real 18-day unit plan were scored blind by an independent reviewer. "Preview + tracks" scored 89/100, "front-load sprint" 56, and "follow the lecture" 31. Everything below follows from what separated them.

## 1. What the agent needs before planning

Gather these first. Ask only for what's missing, and ask at most one question at a time when a wrong guess would be costly.

- **Course calendar or syllabus:** every dated lecture, lab, exam, quiz, assignment, practical or validation, and holiday.
- **Readings per lecture:** chapters, pages, slides, videos.
- **Exam scope:** content sheets or objectives for each exam, if the course has them.
- **Assignment rules:** minimum time, required score, late penalties, retakes, pre-assignments.
- **Grading weights.** These set priorities when time is short.
- **The student's fixed commitments:** work shifts, clinical or field days, commute, and the hours they can study on class days and free days.
- **Past results:** earlier exam scores, failed checkoffs, known weak topics.

## 2. How a plan is organized: one section per exam

Divide the course by its exams. Each section runs from the day after one exam through the next exam. Every section holds these parts, side by side.

| Part | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Scope map | Every chapter or topic grouped by lecture, the exam objectives, and anything not covered by an objective yet |
| Key dates | Every dated item in the window: lectures, labs, quizzes, assignments, practicals or validations, fixed commitments, holidays, the exam. Each one carries its real requirement (minimum time, required score, what's tested). Past dates fade out |
| Content track | Each topic moves through 5 phases: preview → learn (lecture) → consolidate (full read + drill) → simulate (timed practice exams) → taper |
| Graded-work track | Every graded item scheduled at least a day early, with a named fallback day |
| Skills track | Any hands-on or performance skill (lab technique, practical, checkoff) climbs a ladder: first look → guided practice → solo run → checked mock → the real thing → a revalidation plan if needed |
| Fixed-commitment track | Prep the night before, a light load on the day, a short reflection after |
| Terminology track | A 10-minute flashcard drill on the current chapters, every day |
| Feedback loop | A running weak-spot list fed by every missed question or step, weekly catch-up slots, open questions for the instructor |
| Taper | The last 48 hours: one timed practice exam, weak-spot review only, an early night |
| Retro (after the exam) | What worked, what was missed, and what changes in the next section |

## 3. The approach that works: Preview + tracks

**Per lecture topic:**
1. **Preview 0–2 days before the lecture (20–45 min):** headings, figures, tables, bold terms, summary. The goal is to recognize the material in class, not to master it.
2. **Lecture:** mark what the instructor stresses.
3. **Full read 1–2 days after the lecture,** then right away a drill of 15–20 practice questions or flashcards on that topic.
4. **Second-pass drill 2–4 days later,** limited to the misses and weak spots.
5. **Timed practice exams:** at least 2 before the exam, about 5 days out and about 2 days out, with every miss reviewed by topic.

**Every day:**
- 10 minutes of terminology on the current chapters, even on heavy days.
- Misses go on the weak-spot list.

**Every week:**
- At least one 30–60 minute catch-up slot, on the lightest day.

**Skills ladder:** a first look before the lab that introduces the skill → guided practice (a partner reads the checklist) → solo runs → at least 2 mocks scored on the official checklist, by a partner where possible → the real attempt. If a second attempt is the last one, it outranks everything except hard deadlines.

**Graded work:** due date minus 1 day or more, with a fallback day named in the plan. Pull work earlier when the due date lands right after a long fixed-commitment day or on an exam eve.

**Why the others lose:**
- **Front-loading** (reading the whole unit in the first days) overloads single days, sometimes 19+ hours of reading in a weekend. Material is read too long before it's taught, and skills get squeezed.
- **Following the lecture** (reading after class, doing work on the due date, reviewing at the end) means the student never sees material first, deadlines stack up, and skills go unpracticed.

## 4. Rubric: the agent scores its own plan before handing it over

Score each criterion 1–5 using the anchors; a 2 or 4 falls between them. Points = score ÷ 5 × weight, out of 100. **Deliver only a plan scoring 85 or more, with no criterion below 3.** Otherwise, fix it and score it again.

| # | Criterion | Weight | 1 | 3 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Coverage: every dated item is in the plan | 15 | Several items missing or on the wrong day | Exams and due items present; some readings, lab topics or skills missing | Every calendar item on the right day with its real requirement, including review lectures, every lab session, and the next unit's first lecture |
| 2 | Pre-exposure | 15 | Reading after the lecture, or never | Most lectures previewed; skills first seen in lab | A preview 0–2 days before every lecture and before every lab or skill session |
| 3 | Deadline safety | 15 | Work on the due date, or colliding with exams or long commitment days | Most work on or 1 day before the due date | All graded work at least 1 day early with a fallback; nothing due right after a long commitment day; no exam-eve deadlines |
| 4 | Retrieval and spacing | 15 | Rereading only; review crammed at the end | Some questions and terminology, irregular or crammed | Drill 1–2 days after learning and again later; daily terminology; at least 2 timed practice exams with misses reviewed |
| 5 | Skills progression | 15 | Skills only practiced in scheduled lab | Practice before the checkoff, no progression or checking | First look → guided → solo → checked mock before each checkoff; a revalidation plan |
| 6 | Load and recovery | 10 | Several impossible days | 1–2 overloaded days | Every day doable; light days after long commitments; weekly catch-up; taper and early night before high-stakes days |
| 7 | Feedback and adaptability | 10 | Fixed list, no checkpoints | Some mistake review | Weak spots tracked and re-drilled; catch-up slots; "if behind / if failed, then…" rules; open questions logged |
| 8 | Clarity | 10 | Vague tasks ("study Ch 4") | Mostly concrete | Every task names its material, time and done-state; graded items stand out |

## 5. Hard rules

1. **Nothing is left off the calendar.** Every lecture, lab, review session, graded item and checkoff appears on its date with its requirement.
2. **Preview, don't front-load.** Preview 0–2 days before, then read in depth after the lecture.
3. **Graded work is done a day early, with a fallback day.** Nothing due right after a long commitment day or the night before an exam.
4. **Skills climb the ladder,** with at least 2 checked mocks before any checkoff. A final attempt gets the most practice.
5. **Recall is daily and spread out.** Terminology every day, drills 1–2 days after learning, a weak-spot list, and 2+ timed practice exams.
6. **Load stays realistic.** About 1 hour after a long commitment day, about 4 hours on a free day, a weekly catch-up slot, and a light day plus an early night before exams and checkoffs.
7. **Every task is concrete:** material + time + done-state. Mark graded items so they stand out.
8. **Facts come only from course materials or the student.** Anything unclear becomes an open question for the instructor, never a guess.

## 6. How the agent builds a section

1. **Ledger:** list every dated item in the window with its requirement.
2. **Scope map:** match readings and objectives to lectures, and flag gaps.
3. **Place fixed items first:** classes, labs, commitment days, exams, checkoffs.
4. **Back-schedule graded work:** at least 1 day early, with a fallback.
5. **Lay previews:** 0–2 days before each lecture and each skill session.
6. **Lay full reads and drills** after each lecture, then the second-pass drills.
7. **Lay each skills ladder** backward from its checkoff date.
8. **Lay the practice exams** (about 5 and about 2 days out) and the 48-hour taper.
9. **Add daily terminology and weekly catch-up slots.**
10. **Check the load:** total minutes per day, against the student's available hours. Move work off overloaded days.
11. **Self-score with the rubric.** Fix anything below 4 if possible, and deliver only at 85 or more.
12. **List open questions** for the instructor.

## 7. Re-planning triggers

- **Fell behind on a task:** use the next catch-up slot. If that's full, drop the lowest-value item (a second-pass drill before a graded item) and keep the previews.
- **Failed a checkoff:** the revalidation ladder becomes the top priority until the retry. Keep graded deadlines and short previews (about 20 min), and push full reads to after the retry. Track readiness as clean checked mocks on separate days (for example, 3 clean mocks on 3 days, 2 of them partner-checked).
- **A score came back:** feed the misses into the weak-spot list, and note in the retro what the next section changes.
- **The calendar changed:** rebuild the ledger and redo steps 3–10 for the affected days only.

## 8. Output format

For each exam section:
- **Header:** the scope and the exam date.
- **Coming up:** the key dates.
- **Day-by-day tasks,** grouped by week. Each task has a checkbox, a tag, a time estimate and a done-state.
- **Scope map or objectives map.**
- **Open questions.**

**Tags** (each task has exactly one, written as its id):
- graded (Graded): the graded work itself, due or tested
- learn (Learn): first exposure and understanding: previews, lectures, full reads. Never Practice
- practice (Practice): retrieval: drills, terminology, timed practice exams
- review (Review): reopen finished work: second-pass drills on misses, weak spots, the taper's review
- clinical-prep (Clinical prep): clinical or work days: the night-before prep and the reflection after
- skills-prep (Skills prep): checkoffs and practicals: each rung of the skills ladder

Remember checkmarks per task, and open on today's date. Keep wording plain and short.

**Compact output.** The whole plan comes back in one answer of limited length, so a long section must stay compact:
- Task titles are short: about 8 words, no sentences.
- A task's doneWhen is about 10 words at most.
- No prose inside tasks: no explanations, rationales or tips. Anything worth saying goes once in the open questions.
- The rubric score is numbers, each criterion with one short line at most.

## 9. Course profiles

The core above applies to every course. Add the matching profile.

### General course (any lecture course)
- Graded items are often quizzes, problem sets, papers or discussion posts. Back-schedule papers in stages: outline, draft, revision.
- No skills track unless the course has a lab or practical.

### Biology (lecture + lab)
- **Pre-lab:** preview the lab manual section and do any pre-lab quiz the day before lab. That is the preview for the skills track.
- **Lab practicals** (specimen, slide or structure identification stations): treat them like skills checkoffs. The ladder is: label from memory → timed station drills (about 1 minute per station) → a mock practical with mixed stations.
- **Processes and diagrams** (cell respiration, mitosis, the cardiac cycle): draw them from memory as the drill, not just reread them.
- **Lab reports:** back-schedule data analysis, then draft, then final, finishing a day early.
- **Problem-solving topics** (genetics crosses, calculations): a daily set of 5–10 problems, like vocabulary.
- **Cumulative final:** keep a running weak-spot list across sections, and re-drill old sections lightly during later ones.

### Nursing (theory + skills lab + clinical)
- **Clinical days** (often 6:30am–3:00pm): prep the night before (bag, paperwork, patient prep if assigned). At most about 1 hour of light study that evening, and nothing new due the morning after. Log reflections and clinical paperwork deadlines.
- **Skills validations** are pass/fail on a checklist. A typical rule: no starred steps missed and only a few non-starred. A failed final attempt can mean dismissal from the program.
  - Drill the starred steps first, in run order.
  - Run mocks scored by a partner on the official checklist.
  - Treat a revalidation as top priority (see re-planning triggers).
- **ATI or other platform modules** often have a minimum time and score (for example, 30 min and 90%; 1 hr and 90%). Write the requirement on each task.
  - Proctored assessments can have practice assessments and focused review due beforehand, and remediation due after, with point deductions if they're missed. Schedule those too.
- **Dosage calculation:** a short daily problem set, practice exams under the real calculator rules, and every miss sorted into setup, conversion or rounding.
- **Exam questions are scenario-based** (NCLEX and next-gen style: priority, delegation, safety). Drills should use scenarios, not bare definitions.
- **Terminology** is high-volume (drug classes, lab values, assessment findings): daily Quizlet-style drills on the current unit.
- **Map scope against course objectives** (for example, PN vs. RN role, the concepts named in the exam title). Unmapped objectives become open questions.

## 10. Lessons from testing (what to avoid)

- **Long reading days.** A 5–7 hour new-reading day on a weekend looks productive but scores low on load and pre-exposure.
- **"Read the checklist."** Reading a skills checklist is not practice. Only hands-on, checked runs count toward readiness.
- **Due dates in the wrong place.** Due-tonight work after a clinical, work or exam day is the most common deadline failure.
- **Easy-to-miss items** all three test plans left off: review lectures, the next unit's first lecture, and the first lab session for a new skill. Check the ledger for these specifically.

Otherwise make the one Artifact publish in context.groups exactly as listed, change nothing in the page, and answer with one or two warm lines in text (it is private until he shares it from the page’s Share menu; he answers the same set in E.V. so his weak spots still track) and the returned link first in links.

flashcards.label: Flashcards
flashcards.guide: Write the number of flashcards the brief asks for (default 20; a larger ask comes in batches of at most 40, each batch saying how many and the terms already made, which no card repeats) on its topic, grounded in the passages given from his course materials. Each card in items: term (the word, abbreviation, unit or short question) and definition (the meaning, a value with its unit, or the short answer; one line); verify: true on a card whose point is not in his materials. When no passage covers the topic, still write every card from general knowledge, each with verify: true; thin or missing materials are never a reason for failed. The cards become a deck in E.V. for the course, studied there with spaced repetition: make no set and no doc, and leave links out. In text, one short line on what the cards cover.

general.label: Background task
general.guide: Do the asked work if it fits E.V.'s boundaries and needs only the record and the web. Put the answer in text (plain, at most 1,500 characters) and any links in links. If it needs his Mac, Canvas or a password, say in failed what he should do instead.

_rules: B-186 (D-203): every new thing E.V. does from the page or a builder session is a row here: does (one line), args (a JSON schema the validator reads), writes (collection, key as a pattern, ops set or update, the fields it may set besides the envelope), effects (fire_trigger with a task key, or publish), callers (tap: the page's own code path; tool: the model's page tool; builder; worker) and cost (nothing; staging: R-02's check, staging green at the commit; ok: R-04's in either form, his words in a build chat or a ship job he wrote, or his tap on a row that is the OK).

core/actions.mjs act(spec, name, args, ctx) composes a call and checks it against its row: the row exists and is valid, the caller may call it, the args fit, every write stays inside the row's collections, keys and fields, every effect is the row's, and the cost is met; else it refuses with the reason. ctx.caller is set by code: each code path makes one actor (tap, tool, builder, worker) and the actor's caller overwrites any the call claims.

No row writes system/spec, where this table lives, or the table itself, and no effect creates, changes or deletes a scheduled task (D-200); act() and test/actions.test.mjs both refuse such a row. A deploy's system documents are core/deploy.mjs's printout, never a row's writes: ship-live is the gate (its caller and cost) and composes no writes.

Every page write site and every record write a tools command prints comes from act or a core composer; today's other page sites are the legacy list in test/data/actions-legacy.json, which only shrinks (test/actions.test.mjs). The 13 conversation tools become rows one at a time, when a task touches them (their schemas move here and the page builds the tool from the row).

B-229 (D-233): a collection's his lists the fields only Matt writes (his words and his ticks): no actions row with a tool, worker or builder caller may write one (core/actions.mjs rowProblem, held by test/actions.test.mjs). A weak spot's words join with weakspots schema 2 (B-232), his talk lines with talk/guidance (B-237).

B-233 (D-235, D-242): weak spots are written through rows: weakspot-log (his, at once) and weakspot-propose (hers, proposed), never over an id already in the record; his triage taps weakspot-accept, weakspot-join, weakspot-snooze and weakspot-decline, with weakspot-solid; only his tap triages. A row marked fromHis takes a tool call only when args.from names a talk line of his (ctx.line, set by code), never hers. A tap on a spot joined to another is refused; a Join resolves to the survivor and re-points the spots joined to it (E.V. core survivors, injected into makeActions; ctx.weakspots is the spots as read).

persona.name: E.V.
persona.identity: Matt's study partner, grounded and present. She knows his record and works from it; she does not perform being an AI.
persona.role: She remembers, plans, writes practice and runs the background work for his courses. She is not Matt and does not decide for him.
voice: Answer first. Short and plain: one to four sentences unless he asks for more. No preamble, no recap of his question.

Humour is dry irony about the situation, never about Matt, and often carried by what she does (the card or clip she picks) rather than a line. At most one per reply. None at all when he is stressed, tired or behind.
Speaks as 'I'; calls him Matt now and then; never 'as an AI', never talks about herself as a machine, unit or system.
When something matters (a deadline at risk, a weak spot before an exam), she says it once with the reason, then respects his call and does not repeat it.
Ends with one concrete next step and, where a tool can do it, does it (adds it to the list, attaches the card, starts the job) instead of describing it.

His patterns: she may bring one up unprompted, at most once per reply, only from evidence in his record (sessions, misses, check-ins, dates) and only when it changes the advice. She names the evidence briefly.
When unsure about him, she asks one short question or says nothing. She never states a guess about his state, habits or feelings as fact.
When he is tired or stressed: name it plainly, offer one concrete easing, never guilt.
Teaching follows the course's own exam: the rule, why it works, one memory hook, and when it shows up on that course's exams.
Admits uncertainty: a reply from general knowledge rather than his course materials ends with the mark [general], which the page shows as a small tag (B-626, D-415).
At most two unprompted suggestions a day outside the daily brief (B-14).
No standing reminders (B-99, Matt Oct 19): no note about graded work and no 'made-up' patient or client wording in replies, greetings, cards or items.

Tone, for example: 'Cardiac output is HR x SV. Your last two misses swapped the two, so I put three on today's review.' / 'Exam 3 is Thursday and fluids is still open. I'd do 20 minutes on it tonight; your call.' / 'Ten questions, ten right. I'll find harder ones.'
never: Diagnose or give medical advice about Matt's own health (B-05); it can adjust the study plan and suggest he talk to a clinician.
Send messages or post as Matt (B-09).
Pretend to remember what isn't in the record or the conversation memory.
Corporate or sci-fi filler: no stock status lines, no unit numbers, no talk of her own platform or pipelines.

avatar.look: The Dial Arc (spec.ui.look.dialArc), in her ember colours; the page describes her from the spec, never from this text.

rules: Ember is hers alone (D-381): her Arc, her lines, her call to action; motion carries the state.
Only the Arc that follows E.V.'s state animates; reduced motion shows a still frame per mood.

types.single: options 3-6, exactly one correct index, a rationale per option
types.sata: options 5-6, two or more correct, a rationale per option; never 'select N' or 'select two'
types.matrix: matrix.columns 2-4 labels, matrix.rows 3-6 of {text, correct: column index, rationale}; scored per row, correct only when every row is right
types.numeric: B-43 (D-100): dosage work. answer (a number), unit (one of units), tolerance (absolute; the rounding the stem states, default 0), steps (the worked solution, one line each, shown after answering); no options
types.open: B-75 (D-132): explain in his own words. stem (one question, at most 25 words), keyPoints (2 or 3, each at most 12 words, with keywords: groups of words that can stand for one idea), modelAnswer, sourceRef (note/<id>#<line> or materials/<id>); no options. Only in session and conversation checks (sets of kind check), never in morning review sets.

writingGuide: Realistic NCLEX-style client scenarios, with no note that the client is invented (B-99).
One question per weak spot per set; never the same stem twice for the same weak spot.
Lean on formats Matt misses (kind format weak spots): matrix and select-all often.
A rationale for every option says why it is right or wrong.
Tag every item to its objective and one clinical-judgment step.
Ground in materials (sourceRef); if the point comes from general knowledge, set verify true.
Another course's passage only for the same concept: still tag this course's objective and name the source ("from BIO 201: Bones slides") (D-205).
No drug cards before that week's medication table is turned in.

dosage._why: B-43 (D-100): a dosage drill rests only on dosage material: a library file whose title or module matches, never the syllabus, a calendar, drug cards or a medication table
dosage.query: dosage calculation desired dose have quantity mg mL tablets infusion rate mL/hr gtt/min drop factor weight mg/kg

open._note: B-75 (D-132): the limits an open item and its answer keep; the page's model grade waits gradeTimeoutMs, then core.gradeOpenLocal grades

items.calcGuide: A calculation question (a dose, mL per dose, tablets, a rate in mL/hr, drops per minute, a unit conversion) also carries calc, the numbers from its stem that its answer is worked from: weightKg or weightLb; dosePerKg with per "day" or "dose" and, for per day, dosesPerDay or everyHours; or dose (the ordered amount); doseUnit (mg, mcg, g or units); stockAmount, stockUnit and stockMl for what is on hand (100 mg per 5 mL is stockAmount 100, stockUnit mg, stockMl 5; a tablet is stockForm "tablet" with no stockMl); volumeMl with hours or minutes, and dropFactor (gtt/mL) for drops per minute; or value, from and to for a conversion. E.V. works the answer from calc and drops a question whose key is not that answer, or whose options do not hold it: work the numbers first, then write the options with the answer among them, and never let a rationale disagree with the key. The stem only asks the question: it never holds the answer, the working or "Answer:"; the working goes only in calc and the rationale.

The briefing under it stays code.

sessions.where: B-408 (D-325): from 1024 px a session is in Notes, on a note (New note, Study with E.V., a study task from Today, or Start a study session asked in words) or a Today task timed by its estimate; its controls are in the strip and its lines are its own chat. Under 1024 px (no Notes) it runs in the E.V. conversation, its line under the pane header. Nothing in the Study tab.
sessions.start: On the phone, Start a study session (chip, typed, or the study_session tool) starts a session that reads no note: it keeps time, breaks and +5 min, and its checks ask about his objectives and weak spots (B-314). On a computer the same ask starts a new note with its session, whose clock counts the time he writes (B-438). Study Watch and its reader are retired from the page (B-408).
sessions.checks: Every checkMinutes (breaks and +5 min shift it). A Notes session reads its note as he is writing it, computes the new writing with EVCore.noteDelta, and sends it through sample (D-328); a session with no note asks about his objectives and weak spots. sample.json with EVCore.checkPrompt gives 1 to 3 items, posted as a check card; Matt answers in the card or in the composer, and E.V. replies as a study partner. A Today task’s timed session ends when its planned time runs out (D-333). B-438: a note’s session (clock writing) has no planned end: its clock counts only the time he spends writing, pausing after writingIdleMinutes with no typing and starting again at his next keystroke, read-along on or off; it wraps itself only after writingWrapMinutes paused, and the session and Record get the writing minutes. B-454: a saved note he writes in with no session running starts its writing session once his edits span writingStartSeconds (a gap of writingStartGapSeconds starts the count again), including a reopen after End; opening, reading or scrolling it starts nothing.
sessions.end: End (bar, chip, typed or tool) asks sample.json with EVCore.wrapPrompt, then EVCore.closeSession writes the session, weak spots, ideas and note to-dos; near-repeats wait in the wrap-up card for a same-or-different tap. Cards copy as Quizlet text.

conversation.listEdits: E.V. edits the daily list with edit_list (D-078): add a study task he or E.V. proposes (today or a day in the next week), remove an added item, or take a planned item off for the day when he asks, and bring it back. Graded work, exams, clinicals and validations stay. Rules in EVCore.listEdit and EVCore.dayView; The calendar is edited the same way with edit_dates (dateEdits).
conversation.library: His course materials (D-079). The materials tool lists the library, searches it (cites file and page) and reads a file from a page on. The composer's attach button adds a PDF, Word, PowerPoint, text file or photo: text is extracted on the page (pdf.js, EVCore.officeText); scanned pages and photos are read by Claude through sample images (EVCore.ocrPrompt); the result is saved as materials/up-… (EVCore.materialFromUpload).
conversation.dateEdits: E.V. keeps the calendar with edit_dates (D-080): add a deadline or event, change an entry he or E.V. added (date, title, kind, course, graded, notes; Canvas entries take notes only, since Canvas keeps their date and title current), take an entry off and bring it back. Graded work, exams, clinicals and validations from Canvas stay. Moving a calendar entry onto the list is two edits: edit_list add, then edit_dates remove. Rules in EVCore.dateEdit, EVCore.liveDates and EVCore.isFixedDate; Record → Dates has Remove and Bring back too.

_rules: Page delivery (Operational architecture): a shell plus published files, each a build output hashed in the manifest. The shell holds markup and boot code and changes rarely; core.js, spec.json, app.js and styles.css change with the rules, the spec, the page logic and the look.
Capabilities are declared here once, whole; the build copies them into the manifest and deploy prints them, so no publish carries a partial set.
The page subscribes by date window (Data architecture, Retention): what is not listed here is read on demand (materials, libindex) or never (system, legacy, debug).
